title: Lithium-sulfur shuttle effect and cycle life
bottleneck: Lithium-sulfur batteries offer up to 5x the theoretical energy density of lithium-ion using abundant sulfur, but soluble polysulfides shuttle between electrodes, causing rapid capacity fade. Typical cells last 300 to 500 cycles versus the 3,000-plus needed for grid use. Sulfur's 80 percent volume expansion during cycling destroys electrode structure, and self-discharge runs 8 to 15 percent per month. Electrolyte additives that suppress the shuttle effect tend to increase viscosity and cost while reducing ionic conductivity.
why_it_blocks: Li-S has tantalizing energy density but grid storage buys cycle life above all. Five-hundred-cycle batteries are consumables, not infrastructure.
current_state: Research on solid-state and confined-sulfur designs continues. No Li-S cell has demonstrated grid-relevant cycle life. Aviation and drone applications may adopt Li-S first, where energy density matters more than cycle life.
